cases.title: Alice Silva -- Construction Spending Time Series
cases.background: Alice Silva is a quantitative analyst focusing on the real estate sector. Silva studies the extent to which private construction spending is affected by public construction spending. She collects data (in $ millions) on total private (PRIV) and public (PUBL) construction spending for the last 363 months and log-transforms both time series. To determine whether the two log-transformed time series are cointegrated, Silva tests the following null hypotheses: Null Hypothesis 1: ln(PRIVt) has a unit root. Null Hypothesis 2: ln(PUBLt) has a unit root. Null Hypothesis 3: The error term of the linear regression between ln(PRIVt) and ln(PUBLt) has a unit root. Silva forecasts future private construction spending. She estimates an autoregressive model of order 1 (AR(1)), where dln(PRIVt) = ln(PRIVt) - ln(PRIVt-1), using the estimates in Exhibit 1 to determine the mean-reverting level of dln(PRIVt). Next, Silva estimates an AR(1) model for public construction spending, where dln(PUBLt) = ln(PUBLt) - ln(PUBLt-1). She calculates the residuals (e) and squared residuals (e^2) of the AR(1) model and estimates two linear regressions: Residual Regression 1: et = a0 + a1*et-1 + ut; Residual Regression 2: et^2 = a0 + a1*et-1^2 + ut. The t-statistic for the slope coefficients (a1) is 0.70 for Residual Regression 1 and 2.94 for Residual Regression 2. The relevant critical value for these tests is 1.97. Finally, Silva develops a sentiment indicator for the real estate market. She obtains text data from real estate listings and classifies each listing as 'hot,' 'medium,' or 'cold' based on how quickly the property sold. After preparing and wrangling the unstructured data, she performs feature selection. She wants to remove noise features and only select the tokens that tend to occur more often in a particular class of text.

cases.title: Sebastian Moreno -- ML, Logistic Regression and Model Fit
cases.background: Sebastian Moreno is an analyst analyzing probabilities of default for bond issuers and the drivers of ROE. He is tasked with a project to classify bond issuers by their probability of default within the next 12 months. He gathers financial and accounting metrics for 1,000 issuers and observes that the issuers are not linearly separable. He compares non-linear support vector machine (SVM), unconstrained classification and regression tree (CART), and SVM with soft margin classification. He wants an algorithm that addresses non-linear separability and is not prone to overfitting. Moreno also creates Model 1, a logistic regression using two factors, profit margin (PROFIT) and leverage ratio (LEVER), to predict probability of default. The binary dependent variable is 1 for companies that defaulted within the subsequent 12 months and 0 otherwise. Using Exhibit 1, he calculates the predicted probability of default for the average distressed company, which has PROFIT = -2.0 and LEVER = 3.0. To analyze drivers of ROE for software companies, Moreno compares two linear regressions. Model 2 uses profit margin (PROFIT) and interest coverage (COVER). Model 3 extends Model 2 by adding a third factor, the quick ratio (QUICK). He compares the R-squared and adjusted R-squared of the two models; results for Model 3 are in Exhibit 2. Finally, Moreno tests if last-12-month sales (SALES) are a good predictor of ROE with Model 4: ROEi = b0 + b1*SALESi + ei. A plot of the regression residuals against SALES shows the variance of residuals increasing as SALES increase.

cases.title: Danny Aoun -- ML Metrics and Time-Series Forecasting
cases.background: Danny Aoun is an equity portfolio manager developing sentiment indicators for forecasting stock price movements. Aoun then applies his models to two semiconductor stocks, Bytewave and Circuitcraft. For Bytewave, Aoun estimates a first-order autoregressive model (AR(1)) on the stock price and concludes the model exhibits autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity with ARCH(1) errors. For Circuitcraft, Aoun predicts growth in quarterly sales using 13 years of quarterly data, running a regression on the first difference of quarterly sales growth in an AR(2) model. After reviewing the first-differenced data, he determines the mean and variance are constant over time and concludes the time series does not have a unit root. Historical quarterly sales growth: Sales Growth50 = 18.9%, Sales Growth49 = 2.0%, Sales Growth48 = -11.5%. The critical value for the t-statistic is 2.0 at the 5% significance level. Exhibit 2 shows results from this regression.

cases.title: Richard Smith -- Growth Accounting and Convergence

Smith shows that the growth accounting equation decomposes the percentage change in output into components attributable to capital, labor, and technology. Team Blue is asked to calculate the economy's potential growth rate using the growth accounting method with: growth rate of capital = 2.0%, growth rate of labor = 0.5%, growth rate of total factor productivity = 1.0%, share of capital in GDP = 30%. Team Purple investigates whether the per capita income of a developing country should converge toward that of developed countries, reviewing the saving rate, population growth rate, the shape of the production function, and the externalities associated with human capital, and concludes that the externalities associated with human capital is the most important determinant in predicting convergence. Smith concludes that opening up the economy should increase the rate at which countries' capital-to-labor ratios converge, and Team Orange provides three descriptions of the dynamic adjustment process: Description 1 -- the growth in the capital-exporting countries will be above the steady state; Description 2 -- developed countries will tend to run trade deficits as they export capital; Description 3 -- the rate of return on investments will be lower in countries with high capital-to-labor ratios.

questions.los: Cointegration: unit-root tests on two series plus Engle-Granger test on regression residuals
questions.stem: The time series ln(PRIVt) and ln(PUBLt) are cointegrated if the tests performed by Silva:

choices.C: fail to reject all three null hypotheses.

explanations.A: Correct. To be cointegrated, two time series must both have a unit root (fail to reject Null Hypotheses 1 and 2 by a Dickey-Fuller test) AND the residuals of the regression between them must not have a unit root (reject Null Hypothesis 3 by an Engle-Granger Dickey-Fuller test). Only this scenario (both series have a unit root and the error term of the regression does not) corresponds to cointegration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rejecting Null Hypotheses 1 and 2 would mean neither series has a unit root, so they cannot be cointegrated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Failing to reject Null Hypothesis 3 means the regression error term has a unit root, so the series are not cointegrated (Scenario 5).

questions.los: AR(1) mean-reverting level = b0/(1-b1)
questions.stem: The mean-reverting level of dln(PRIVt) is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.002 is roughly the intercept b0 alone; the mean-reverting level divides by (1 - b1).
explanations.B: Correct. The mean-reverting level of the dependent variable of an AR(1) model is b0/(1 - b1) = 0.00259/(1 - 0.38616) = 0.0042.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.387 is the slope coefficient b1, not the mean-reverting level.

steps.label: Trap
steps.content: Do not report b0 (0.002) or b1 (0.387) directly.

questions.los: ARCH(1) test: regress squared residuals on one lag of squared residuals
questions.stem: Do the estimates of the residual regression parameters indicate that the AR(1) model on dln(PUBLt) is misspecified?

choices.B: Yes, because there is evidence of significant serial correlation
choices.C: Yes, because there is evidence of autoregressive conditional heteroskedasticity (ARCH)

explanations.A: Incorrect. Residual Regression 2 indicates the model exhibits ARCH, hence it is not well specified.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no evidence of significant serial correlation: the slope of Residual Regression 1 (t = 0.70) is not statistically different from 0, so we cannot reject the null that the residuals are not autocorrelated.
explanations.C: Correct. Engle's test regresses the squared residuals on a constant and one lag of the squared residuals (et^2 = a0 + a1*et-1^2 + ut); if a1 is significant the series is ARCH(1). For Residual Regression 2 the t-statistic on a1 is 2.94 > critical value 1.97, so the model exhibits ARCH and is misspecified.

questions.los: Feature selection for text data: mutual information
questions.stem: To perform feature selection, Silva should select the tokens with the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Tokens with the lowest term frequency are likely noise features, which Silva wants to remove, not select.
explanations.B: Correct. Mutual information measures how much information a token contributes to a class of text. Tokens that occur more often in a particular class have high MI; selecting the highest-MI tokens keeps the informative features and removes noise.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Highest document frequency tends to identify very common tokens that appear across all classes and carry little discriminating information.

questions.los: Algorithm selection: SVM soft margin for non-linear separability without overfitting
questions.stem: Which of the following machine-learning algorithms is most suitable for Moreno's bond issuer classification model?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Non-linear SVM introduces more complex non-linear separation boundaries; it may reduce training misclassifications but is more complex and prone to overfitting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An unconstrained CART makes no assumptions about the training data and can perfectly learn (overfit) it; avoiding overfitting requires regularization such as maximum depth or minimum node population.
explanations.C: Correct. SVM with soft margin classification handles non-linear separability by adding a penalty to the objective function for misclassified training observations, optimizing the trade-off between a wider margin and a lower total error penalty, and is less prone to overfitting.

questions.los: Adding a variable: R^2 and adjusted R^2 behavior (t-stat rule of |1.0|)
questions.stem: Compared to Model 2, Model 3 most likely has a:

choices.A: lower R-squared and a higher adjusted R-squared.
choices.B: higher R-squared and a lower adjusted R-squared.
choices.C: higher R-squared and a higher adjusted R-squared.

explanations.A: Incorrect. R-squared cannot decrease when a variable is added.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adjusted R-squared decreases only if the added variable's t-statistic is below |1.0|; here QUICK has t = 1.9204 > 1.0.
explanations.C: Correct. As independent variables are added, R-squared increases or stays the same. Adjusted R-squared rises if the new coefficient's t-statistic exceeds |1.0| and falls if it is below |1.0|. QUICK's t-statistic is 1.9204, so adjusted R-squared for Model 3 is higher than for Model 2.

questions.los: Conditional heteroskedasticity from residual plot; effect on F-test reliability
questions.stem: The most appropriate conclusion to draw from the residual plot for Model 4 is that:

choices.A: the model suffers from unconditional heteroskedasticity.
choices.B: there is a non-linear relationship between ROE and SALES.
choices.C: the F-test for the overall regression significance is unreliable.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Unconditional heteroskedasticity occurs when the error variance is NOT correlated with the independent variables and creates no major inference problems. Here the residual variance rises with SALES, so the variance is correlated with the regressor -- this is conditional, not unconditional, heteroskedasticity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A plot of residuals against a feature does not reveal the nature of the target-feature relationship; the pattern here is about error variance, not non-linearity.
explanations.C: Correct. The residual variance increases with SALES, i.e., the error variance is conditional on the regressor -- conditional heteroskedasticity. This makes the MSE a biased estimator of the true population variance, so the F-test for overall regression significance is unreliable, and it tends to find significant relationships where none exist (more Type I errors).

questions.los: Model evaluation: recall minimizes false negatives (Type II errors)
questions.stem: Which machine-learning model should Aoun choose given his concern about false negatives?

explanations.A: Correct. Recall is the ratio of correctly predicted positives to all actual positives and is the metric to maximize when the cost of false negatives (Type II errors) is high. Model X has the highest recall (0.94 vs 0.90 and 0.82).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Accuracy and F1 score (highest for Model Y) weight false positives and negatives equally; they do not directly address the higher cost of false negatives.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Precision (highest for Model Z) addresses the cost of false positives (Type I errors), the opposite of Aoun's concern.

questions.los: ARCH(1): error variance is time-varying but predictable from prior squared error
questions.stem: Based on Aoun's conclusion regarding the time-series model for Bytewave, the variance of the error term is:

explanations.A: Correct. With ARCH(1) errors, the variance of the error in period t+1 can be predicted in period t because it depends on how large the squared error was in the previous period. Thus the error variance is predictable but not constant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. ARCH errors are by definition not constant (the variance changes with the prior squared error).
explanations.C: Incorrect. ARCH(1) errors are predictable: the variance depends linearly on the previous period's squared error.

questions.los: Covariance stationarity: constant mean, constant variance, constant autocovariance
questions.stem: The first-differenced time series for Circuitcraft's growth in quarterly sales:

explanations.A: Incorrect. In a random walk the best forecast of xt is xt-1. Here b2 = -0.5272 with t = -4.3411 (|t| > 2.0), so b2 is significant and its absolute value is less than 1; xt-1 is not the best forecast in every subsequent period, so the series is not a random walk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Seasonality would show a significant fourth (quarterly) residual autocorrelation. The largest residual autocorrelation t-statistic is 1.8424 (lag 3) < 2.0, so no autocorrelation differs significantly from 0 and there is no seasonality.
explanations.C: Correct. None of the residual autocorrelations differ significantly from 0 (largest |t| = 1.8424 < 2.0), so the autocovariance is constant. Aoun determines the mean and variance are constant over time. All three requirements of a covariance-stationary series (constant mean, constant variance, constant autocovariance) are satisfied.

questions.los: Unsupervised learning: agglomerative (bottom-up hierarchical) clustering
questions.stem: Which of the following machine learning algorithms is most appropriate for Cambo to use when selecting the stocks for the new ETF?

explanations.A: Correct. Agglomerative (bottom-up hierarchical) clustering treats each observation as its own cluster, then iteratively combines the two closest clusters by a similarity measure. Grouping stocks by co-movement similarity of returns with an unknown number of groups is unsupervised learning, making agglomerative clustering the appropriate choice.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Principal components analysis reduces highly correlated features into fewer uncorrelated composite variables; it does not group observations into clusters.

questions.los: Breusch-Pagan test for conditional heteroskedasticity (one-tail chi-square)
questions.stem: If Cambo assumes a significance level of 5%, based on the result of the BP test he should conclude that the:

choices.A: statistics of the independent variables are unreliable.
choices.B: residuals do not exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Because the null is not rejected, the model does not have conditional heteroskedasticity and there is no basis to call the statistics unreliable.
explanations.B: Correct. The Breusch-Pagan test is a one-tail (right-tail) chi-square test with k = 3 degrees of freedom; at the 5% level the critical value is 7.815. Because the BP statistic 5.8 < 7.815, the null is not rejected: the residuals do not exhibit conditional heteroskedasticity and the standard errors are unbiased.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Underestimated standard errors would arise if conditional heteroskedasticity were present; here it is not detected.

questions.los: Classification errors: Type I error (false positive) at the chosen threshold
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 2, the most appropriate statement about the model's performance for the selected credit applicant is that it results in:

questions.los: AR model specification: significant residual autocorrelation implies misspecification

explanations.C: Incorrect. The significant first-lag coefficient is expected in an AR(1) and does not by itself indicate misspecification; the residual autocorrelation does.

questions.los: Dickey-Fuller test: reject H0(g1=0) implies stationary (no unit root)
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 3, the test that Lin conducts for model A:

explanations.C: Incorrect. Leverage can amplify positions (used mostly by quantitative managers), but it is not the primary source of skill; stock selection is.

questions.los: Strategy best suited to limit drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio
questions.stem: Which of the following hedge fund strategies is best suited to meet the plan's drawdown objective?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Event-driven/distressed strategies show high maximum drawdowns when combined with a traditional portfolio and provide little risk reduction.
explanations.B: Correct. When combined with a traditional stock and bond portfolio, opportunistic strategies -- specifically global macro and systematic futures (as well as merger arbitrage and equity market-neutral) -- generate the smallest maximum drawdowns and have low serial autocorrelation (good liquidity), providing risk mitigation even during market stress.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Relative value/convertible arbitrage strategies show high maximum drawdowns and relatively high standard deviations when combined with the traditional portfolio, offering little risk-reduction benefit.

questions.los: Theory of storage: futures > spot implies convenience yield < storage cost
questions.stem: Based on the Theory of Storage, the convenience yield for coffee is:

explanations.A: Correct. The Theory of Storage states futures price = spot price + direct storage costs - convenience yield. Here the coffee futures prices are higher than the spot price, so the convenience yield must be less than the storage cost.
explanations.B: Incorrect. If convenience yield equaled storage cost, the futures price would equal the spot price; here futures exceed spot.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A convenience yield higher than storage cost would make futures prices lower than spot (backwardation); here futures are above spot.

questions.los: Gross roll return = (near contract price - farther contract price)/near contract price
questions.stem: The gross roll return on coffee futures from the August Year 0 contract into the May Year 1 contract is closest to:

questions.los: Neoclassical steady-state growth rate = TFP growth/labor share + labor force growth
questions.stem: Based on the neoclassical model, the steady-state growth rate for Country A is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 3.8% is just the scaled TFP term (2.1%/0.552) without adding labor force growth.
explanations.B: Correct. Under the neoclassical model the steady-state growth rate = TFP growth scaled by the labor share plus labor force growth: 2.1%/0.552 + 0.9% = 3.804% + 0.9% = 4.70%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 5.6% adds labor productivity growth (3.5%) rather than correctly scaling TFP growth by the labor share.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Steady-state growth = theta/(1 - alpha) + n, where 1 - alpha = labor share = 0.552

questions.los: Labor productivity growth accounting: potential GDP growth = labor force growth + labor productivity growth
questions.stem: Based on the labor productivity growth accounting equation, the potential GDP growth rate of Country B is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 2.0% omits part of the sum.
explanations.B: Correct. Growth in potential GDP = growth in the labor force + growth in labor productivity = 0.5% + 2.3% = 2.8%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4.3% double counts by adding TFP growth on top of labor productivity growth.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Potential GDP growth = labor force growth + labor productivity growth

steps.label: Inputs

questions.los: Endogenous growth model: open trade permanently raises the growth rate
questions.stem: Which of the following models would best support Podlasky's conclusion regarding the impact of removing Country A's trade barriers?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The classical model does not predict a permanent increase in per capita growth from open trade.
explanations.B: Incorrect. In the neoclassical model open trade raises the level of output and speeds convergence but does not permanently raise the growth rate.
explanations.C: Correct. Open trade fosters innovation and, through selection, scale, and backwardness effects, endogenous growth models predict that a more open trade policy will permanently raise the rate of economic growth, matching Podlasky's conclusion of a permanent increase in per capita growth.

questions.los: Output gap implications for long-term equity returns and short-term inflation
questions.stem: Podlasky's revisions to the growth forecasts for Country B most likely imply:

choices.A: lower expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.
choices.B: higher expected long-term equity returns and lower expected short-term inflation.
choices.C: higher expected long-term equity returns and higher expected short-term inflation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A higher growth rate in potential GDP implies higher, not lower, long-term equity returns.
explanations.B: Correct. A higher estimated growth rate in potential GDP implies higher long-term equity returns, and a lower estimate of short-term GDP growth (below potential) puts downward pressure on inflation, implying lower expected short-term inflation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Short-term GDP growth below potential puts downward, not upward, pressure on inflation, so expected short-term inflation is lower.

questions.los: Triangular arbitrage: compare dealer cross rate with interbank implied cross rate
questions.stem: Based on the dealer's JPY/EUR quote, is there an arbitrage opportunity for the hedge fund?

choices.B: Yes, by purchasing EUR in the interbank market and selling EUR to the dealer
choices.C: Yes, by purchasing EUR from the dealer and selling EUR in the interbank market

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is an arbitrage: the dealer's EUR offer is cheaper than the interbank implied bid.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This is the opposite of the profitable trade; buying EUR interbank and selling to the dealer would lose money.
explanations.C: Correct. The interbank implied JPY/EUR is 119.4342/119.5550 (USD/EUR times JPY/USD). The dealer quotes 119.38/119.40, so the fund can buy EUR from the dealer at 119.40 and sell EUR in the interbank market at 119.43 for a profit.

questions.los: Covered interest rate parity forward rate
questions.stem: Based on covered interest rate parity, the 6-month forward USD/NZD exchange rate is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.6774 has the interest-rate ratio inverted.
explanations.B: Correct. F(USD/NZD) = S0 * (1 + rUS/2)/(1 + rNZD/2) = 0.6808 * (1 + 0.005/2)/(1 + 0.01/2) = 0.6791. Because NZD has the higher interest rate, it trades at a forward discount.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.6825 applies the rate differential in the wrong direction, implying a forward premium for the higher-yielding currency.

steps.content: F(f/d) = S(f/d) * (1 + i(price)/2)/(1 + i(base)/2) for a 6-month tenor

questions.los: Warning signs of a currency crisis: FX reserves decline relative to FX turnover
questions.stem: Which of the following conditions would most likely be a warning sign of a currency crisis in Country B?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Large inflows of foreign capital typically precede a crisis; Country B shows a slight decline in foreign investment, not an inflow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Broad money growth and the ratio of M2 to bank reserves tend to rise before a crisis; here these indicators have declined.
explanations.C: Correct. Foreign exchange reserves tend to decline precipitously as a crisis approaches. The sizable decline in the ratio of FX reserves to average daily FX turnover is the warning sign present in Country B.

questions.los: Growth accounting (Cobb-Douglas): output growth = TFP + alpha*capital growth + (1-alpha)*labor growth
questions.stem: Based on the information given to Team Blue, the estimate of the economy's potential growth rate is closest to:

explanations.A: Correct. Growth accounting: output growth = TFP growth + alpha*capital growth + (1 - alpha)*labor growth = 1.0% + 0.30*2.0% + 0.70*0.5% = 1.0% + 0.6% + 0.35% = 1.95%.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 2.55% mis-weights capital and labor (for example, applying full weights).
explanations.C: Incorrect. 3.50% sums the raw factor growth rates without applying the income shares.

steps.label: Formula
steps.content: Output growth = TFP + alpha*(capital growth) + (1 - alpha)*(labor growth), alpha = 0.30

questions.los: Capital deepening, TFP measurement, and investment's link to the existing capital stock
questions.stem: Which of the points raised by Team Green is most likely correct?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The relationship between growth and R&D spending is not clear-cut: technological innovation raises output in the long run but can cause cyclical slowing through creative destruction (the double-edged nature of innovation).
explanations.B: Incorrect. The statement is reversed: labor productivity growth equals the contribution of capital deepening plus TFP; capital deepening is measured as the difference between labor productivity growth and TFP growth.
explanations.C: Correct. Although long-term sustainable growth cannot rely on pure capital deepening, the impact of investment spending on available capital depends on the existing physical capital stock, which explains the strong cross-country correlation between investment spending and economic growth (the effect is especially large in developing countries with low capital per worker).

questions.los: Convergence concepts: human-capital externalities imply non-convergence
questions.stem: Which of the following convergence concepts is most compatible with Team Purple's conclusion?

explanations.A: Correct. Emphasizing the externalities associated with human capital implies a linear (straight-line) production function and is compatible with non-convergence: the endogenous growth model makes no prediction that convergence should occur, allowing high-income countries with more capital to stay ahead through high rates of investment in knowledge and human capital.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Absolute convergence assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital, which is inconsistent with strong human-capital externalities.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Conditional convergence also assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital (conditional on the same saving rate, population growth, and production function), inconsistent with the emphasis on human-capital externalities.

questions.los: Capital flows and convergence: adjustment dynamics under open trade
questions.stem: Which of the following descriptions provided by Team Orange is consistent with Smith's conclusion?

explanations.A: Incorrect. During the transition, growth in the capital-exporting (developed) countries will be below, not above, the steady state.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Because capital flows are matched by offsetting trade flows, developed countries that export capital will tend to run trade surpluses, not deficits.
explanations.C: Correct. Developing countries have less capital per worker and a higher marginal product of capital, so the rate of return on investments is higher in low capital-to-labor countries and lower in countries with high capital-to-labor ratios, consistent with Smith's conclusion.

questions.los: Uncovered interest rate parity: expected FX change equals the interest rate differential
questions.stem: Based on uncovered interest rate parity, the expected change in the USD/GBP rate in one year is closest to:

explanations.A: Correct. Under uncovered interest rate parity the expected change in USD/GBP equals the interest rate differential (US minus UK) = 0.55% - 1.75% = -1.2%. Because the UK (base currency) has the higher rate, GBP is expected to depreciate 1.2% against the USD.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The direction is wrong: the higher-yield currency (GBP) is expected to depreciate, so USD/GBP falls.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 1.05% uses an incorrect interest rate differential.

questions.los: Labor productivity growth accounting: potential GDP growth = labor force growth + labor productivity growth
questions.stem: Assume UK's population growth net of immigration is 1 percent for the period 2013-2023. Using the data given above and the labor productivity growth accounting equation, the estimated growth rate in potential GDP is closest to:

explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.3% is just the growth in labor productivity, omitting labor force growth.
explanations.C: Correct. Growth in potential GDP = growth rate of labor force + growth rate in labor productivity = 1% + 0.3% = 1.3%.

questions.los: Endogenous growth model: constant returns to capital (no diminishing returns)
questions.stem: Which of the following is not true according to the endogenous growth model?

choices.A: The economy does not converge to a steady-state rate of growth.
choices.B: Increasing capital will result in diminishing marginal returns.
choices.C: Spending on R&D has positive externalities that benefit the whole economy.

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e., this statement is true). In the endogenous growth model the economy does not converge to a steady-state rate of growth.
explanations.B: Correct (this is the untrue statement). Unlike the neoclassical model, which assumes diminishing marginal returns to capital, endogenous growth models assume investment in capital can have constant returns, so increasing the saving rate can permanently raise the growth rate.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e., this statement is true). R&D spending has positive externalities that benefit the whole economy, a key feature of the endogenous growth model.

questions.los: Triangular arbitrage: dealer overpricing BRL relative to interbank implied cross rate
questions.stem: Based on Exhibit 1, the most appropriate recommendation regarding the triangular arbitrage trade is to:

choices.A: decline the trade, because no arbitrage profits are possible.
choices.B: execute the trade, buy BRL in the interbank market, and sell BRL to the dealer.
choices.C: execute the trade, buy BRL from the dealer, and sell BRL in the interbank market.

explanations.A: Incorrect. An arbitrage exists because the dealer's bid to buy BRL (0.2355) is higher than the interbank implied offer (0.23505).
explanations.B: Correct. The interbank implied CHF/BRL cross rate is 0.2349/0.23505 (CHF/USD times USD/BRL, where USD/BRL is 0.23980/0.23982). The dealer is willing to buy BRL at 0.2355, higher than the 0.23505 at which BRL can be bought in the interbank market, so buy BRL in the interbank market and sell to the dealer for a profit of about 0.0045 CHF per BRL.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses the profitable direction; buying from the dealer and selling interbank would lose money.

questions.los: Covered interest rate parity forward and forward premium (discount)
questions.stem: Based upon Exhibit 2, the forward premium (discount) for a 270-day CAD/GBP forward contract is closest to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. -0.0274 mis-signs or mis-scales the interest rate differential.
explanations.B: Correct. F = S * [1 + i(CAD)*(270/360)]/[1 + i(GBP)*(270/360)] = 1.5872 * (1 + 0.046*0.75)/(1 + 0.013*0.75) = 1.6261. Forward premium = F - S = 1.6261 - 1.5872 = 0.0389. CAD (price currency) has the higher rate, so GBP trades at a forward premium in CAD/GBP terms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. -0.0380 has the wrong sign; the higher CAD rate makes CAD/GBP forward exceed spot.

questions.los: Mundell-Fleming: both expansionary policies leave the currency effect indeterminate
questions.stem: Based on the findings of the Mundell-Fleming model, what is the best possible response to the candidate's Question 1?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Appreciation would follow restrictive monetary and/or expansionary fiscal policy; here both policies are expansionary.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Depreciation would follow expansionary monetary and/or restrictive fiscal policy; here fiscal policy is expansionary, not restrictive.
explanations.C: Correct. Under high capital mobility with flexible exchange rates, the effect on the currency of monetary and fiscal policies that are both expansionary (or both restrictive) is indeterminate, because the monetary expansion pushes the currency down while the fiscal expansion pushes it up.

questions.los: Growth accounting: identify the largest contributor (capital vs labor vs TFP)
questions.stem: Based on the economic data given above and the growth accounting equation, the most appropriate conclusion is that GDP growth is driven by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The labor contribution (1 - alpha)*labor growth = 0.4*1.3 = 0.52% is the smallest of the three.
explanations.B: Correct. Share of capital alpha = 0.6 (since labor share = 0.4). Capital contribution = alpha*capital growth = 0.6*6.2% = 3.72%; TFP = labor productivity growth - capital deepening = 3.4% - 1.7% = 1.7%; labor = 0.4*1.3% = 0.52%. Capital's 3.72% is the largest, so GDP growth is driven by capital.
explanations.C: Incorrect. TFP contributes 1.7%, less than the 3.72% from capital.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.content: Capital's 3.72% is largest -> growth driven by capital
